text: Windows 2000 is a major release of the Windows NT operating system developed by Microsoft, targeting the server and business markets as the direct successor to Windows NT 4.0. It was released to manufacturing on December 15, 1999, and to retail on February 17, 2000 for all versions, with Windows 2000 Datacenter Server released to retail on September 26, 2000. The operating system introduced NTFS 3.0, the Encrypting File System, and support for basic and dynamic disk storage. It improved support for people with disabilities through new assistive technologies and expanded language and locale support. The Windows 2000 Server family included Active Directory, which became widely used in business environments. Although support for the Alpha architecture was present in early development builds, including 64-bit versions, it was discontinued during the final stages of development after Compaq dropped support, and no 64-bit version of Windows 2000 was officially released. The decision to drop the "NT" name from the product line was the result of a debate between Jim Allchin and Bill Gates, with Allchin advocating for modernization and Gates favoring integration with the existing series; Allchin ultimately won. Four editions were released: Professional, Server, Advanced Server, and Datacenter Server, with the latter launched months after the others. All editions share core features such as the Microsoft Management Console and standard system administration tools. Microsoft marketed Windows 2000 as the most secure Windows version at the time, though it faced high-profile virus attacks like Code Red and Nimda. It was succeeded by Windows XP, released on October 2001, and Windows Server 2003, released on April 2003, more than three years after the initial release of Windows 2000 Server. Support for Windows 2000 ended on July 13, 2010, the same day support ended for Windows XP SP2. Both the original Xbox and Xbox 360 used a modified version of the Windows 2000 kernel, with the former's source code leaked in 2020. Originally named Windows NT 5.0, the operating system began development in early 1997 with beta builds identical to Windows NT 4.0, and the first official beta was released in September 1997, followed by Beta 2 in August 1998. On October 27, 1998, Microsoft announced the final name would be Windows 2000, referencing its projected release date. Windows 2000 Beta 3 was released in May 1999, and the new login prompt, icons, and boot screen first appeared in that build. The operating system did not have a codename, as Jim Allchin did not like them; Service Pack 1 was codenamed "Asteroid." Microsoft released three release candidates between July and November 1999, followed by a partner release on December 12, 1999, and manufacturing on December 15, 1999. A leaked memo revealed over 63,000 known defects in the system, though Microsoft claimed it was the most reliable and stable operating system shipped to that point due to mature source code, stress testing, and error detection. InformationWeek and Wired News described the launch as meeting expectations but lacking excitement, and Novell criticized Active Directory as less scalable than its own NDS. Windows 2000 was initially planned to replace both Windows 98 and Windows NT 4.0, but this changed when Windows 98 Second Edition was released in 1999. On or shortly before February 12, 2004, portions of Windows 2000 and Windows NT 4.0 source code were illegally made available online, traced to Mainsoft, and Microsoft issued a statement warning against distribution. An exploit allegedly discovered by someone studying the leaked code was reported on February 16, 2004, and GitHub removed a repository containing Windows NT 4.0 source code on April 15, 2015. Microsoft had planned a 64-bit version for Itanium, codenamed "Janus," but the first officially released 64-bit version was Windows XP 64-Bit Edition, released on October 25, 2001, followed by limited server editions based on pre-release Windows Server 2003 code, released in 2002 and superseded by final Server 2003 versions on April 24, 2003. Windows 2000 incorporated features from Windows 98 and 98 SE, such as the Windows Desktop Update, Internet Explorer 5, Outlook Express, FAT32 support, 3DNow!, SSE, SSE2, Windows Driver Model, Internet Connection Sharing, Windows Media Player 6.4, WebDAV, Bluetooth 1.0, USB device class drivers, and improved FireWire support. It introduced USB 2.0 support in SP4, Wireless Zero Configuration, and SSE3. It was the first Windows version to support hibernation at the OS level (ACPI S4 sleep state). Windows File Protection was introduced to prevent unauthorized modification of critical system files, with the System File Checker allowing manual scans and repairs. A system setting enabled automatic reboot on stop errors, with options to create minidumps or full memory dumps and log events. Administrators could optimize memory and processor usage for background services or applications. Core system administration features like Windows Installer, Windows Management Instrumentation, and Event Tracing for Windows were introduced. A major improvement over Windows NT 4.0 was full Plug and Play with ACPI and Windows Driver Model support, enabling automatic hardware recognition, resource allocation, driver loading, and device notifications. Version 3 print drivers based on Unidrv were introduced, and generic 5-button mouse support was added. Driver Verifier was introduced to detect driver bugs. Windows 2000 introduced layered windows with transparency, translucency, and effects like shadows and alpha-blended GUI elements, and menus supported a Fade transition. The Start menu included personalized menus, expandable special folders, and the ability to launch multiple programs by holding SHIFT, with a Re-sort button to sort by name. The Taskbar supported balloon notifications. Windows Explorer introduced customizable toolbars, auto-complete in the address bar and Run box, advanced file type associations, comments in shortcuts as tooltips, extensible columns, icon overlays, an integrated search pane, sort by name, and a Places bar. Active Desktop, introduced in Internet Explorer 4.0, was included and allowed HTML-based folder customization, though it was exploited by viruses like VBS/Roor-C and VBS.Redlof.a. The "Web-style" folders view with left-pane details and media previews was default, and until Windows Vista, Windows 2000 was the only Windows release with an interactive media player as a default previewer. Default tooltips displayed file title, author, subject, and comments, readable from NTFS streams or OLE structured storage, and all Microsoft Office documents since Office 4.0 displayed this metadata. File shortcuts could store comments displayed as tooltips. The shell introduced extensibility via metadata, icon overlay, and column handlers. The right pane of Explorer could be customized, with system folders showing warnings by default and additional panes defined via DIV elements in folder templates. A DHTML-based search pane was integrated into Explorer, and the Indexing Service was built into the OS, enabling file searches through its database. Windows 2000 also introduced disk quotas, file-system-level encryption, sparse files, and reparse points, with sparse files enabling efficient storage of large data sets with zero-filled areas and reparse points allowing transparent file system functionality changes.

A warning is provided to users that modifying system folder contents could harm their computer. In Windows 2000, additional Explorer panes can be defined using DIV elements in folder template files, a level of customizability not available in Windows 98 or the Desktop Update. The new DHTML-based search pane is integrated into Windows 2000 Explorer, unlike the separate search dialog in earlier versions, and works with the integrated Indexing Service to search files indexed by its database. Microsoft released version 3.0 of NTFS as part of Windows 2000 (sometimes incorrectly called "NTFS 5"), introducing disk quotas (via QuotaAdvisor), file-system-level encryption, sparse files, and reparse points. Sparse files enable efficient storage of large data sets with many zero-filled areas, while reparse points allow the object manager to reset file namespace lookups and enable transparent functionality changes, used for volume mount points, junctions, Hierarchical Storage Management, Native Structured Storage, and Single Instance Storage. Volume mount points and directory junctions allow transparent file references between locations. Windows 2000 introduced Distributed Link Tracking to ensure file shortcuts remain functional if the target is moved or renamed; the target's unique identifier is stored in the shortcut on NTFS 3.0, and the service silently updates the shortcut if the target changes. The Encrypting File System (EFS) provides strong file system-level encryption, allowing transparent encryption of any folder or drive on an NTFS volume. EFS uses a bulk symmetric key (File Encryption Key or FEK) for fast encryption and decryption of large data, which is then encrypted with the user's public key and stored in the file header. Decryption uses the user's private key to retrieve the FEK, which is then used to decrypt the file. EFS includes recovery agents—users authorized by a public key recovery certificate—to decrypt files; by default, local administrators are recovery agents, configurable via Group Policy. Windows 2000 introduced the Logical Disk Manager and diskpart command-line tool for dynamic storage, supporting simple, spanned, and striped volumes in all editions. Windows 2000 Server, Advanced Server, and Datacenter Server also support mirrored volumes and striped volumes with parity. Windows 2000 brought accessibility features from the Windows 9x line to the NT line, including support for visual and auditory impairments, and added new accessibility features. It introduced the Multilingual User Interface (MUI), supporting Arabic, Armenian, Baltic, Central European, Cyrillic, Georgian, Greek, Hebrew, Indic, Japanese, Korean, simplified Chinese, Thai, traditional Chinese, Turkic, and Vietnamese, along with many locales. English versions support right-to-left and CJKV languages, but require installation of related files in Control Panel. Windows 2000 includes DirectX 7.0 and supports up to DirectX 9.0c (Shader Model 3.0), which shipped with Windows XP Service Pack 2; Microsoft released quarterly updates to DirectX 9.0c through February 2010, after which support ended in June 2010, with bug fixes and libraries like D3DX, XAudio 2, XInput, and Managed DirectX. Most DirectX 9.0c games run on Windows 2000. It includes the same games as Windows NT 4.0: FreeCell, Minesweeper, Pinball, and Solitaire. Windows 2000 introduced the Microsoft Management Console (MMC), used to create, save, and open administrative tools; each is a console containing one or more snap-ins, which can be standalone or extensions. Consoles can be created in author mode (allowing snap-in addition, window creation, and saving) or user mode (with restricted access, allowing viewing but not adding snap-ins or multiple windows). The main tools are in the Computer Management console (in Administrative Tools), including Event Viewer, system information, backup utility, Task Scheduler, shared folder management, COM+ configuration, Group Policy, user and group management, device manager, Disk Management, Removable Storage, disk defragmenter, performance diagnostic console, service configuration, and CHKDSK with performance improvements. Two registry editors are included: REGEDIT.EXE, ported from Windows 98 and lacking registry permission editing, and REGEDT32.EXE, which supports permission editing via an older MDI interface and displays keys and values in separate windows. Windows XP later merged both into a single utility. The System File Checker (SFC) is a command-line tool that verifies system file integrity and signs, and can repair files in the Dllcache folder. The Recovery Console runs outside the installed Windows to perform maintenance tasks when booting fails, including commands like fixmbr; it can check, repair drives, restore boot information, replace corrupted files from the CD, or enable/disable services/drivers. It can be accessed via bootable media or other methods. Windows 2000 introduced Windows Script Host 2.0 with an expanded object model and support for logon and logoff scripts. The Windows 2000 Server family includes Windows 2000 Server, Advanced Server, Small Business Server, and Datacenter Server. All server editions include core services and features. Server editions add Microsoft Distributed File System (DFS), Active Directory support, and fault-tolerant storage. DFS groups network shares under a single DFS root, which can only exist on a server version and only one per server. DFS can be implemented as a standalone root (local only, no Active Directory) or domain-based root (within Active Directory, with fault tolerance via replication through the Microsoft File Replication Service). Active Directory replaces Windows NT's domain model with a hierarchical structure, enabling centralized user and computer policy management, automatic program deployment, and scalable user account management; it supports domains from a few hundred to millions of objects, linking domains into trees and forests. Active Directory services can be installed on Server Standard, Advanced, or Datacenter editions but not on Windows 2000 Professional, though Professional is the first client OS to use its features. Active Directory requires a DNS server supporting SRV resource records or upgraded DNS infrastructure, and at least one domain controller to hold the database and provide directory services. Server editions support mirrored volumes and RAID-5 volumes in addition to simple, spanned, and striped volumes. Windows 2000 can be deployed via traditional media (CD) or shared folders, with attended or unattended installations. Unattended installations use an answer file or INI script with pre-filled options, passed to Winnt.exe or Winnt32.exe. Deployment methods include bootable CD, Microsoft Systems Management Server (SMS), System Preparation Tool (Sysprep), Winnt32.exe with /syspart, or Remote Installation Services (RIS). Sysprep allows duplication of a disk image from a reference computer to multiple target servers, with the same HALs, ACPI support, and mass storage devices (though Windows 2000 auto-detects plug and play devices); the Winnt.exe command must include /unattend and /s switches. Sysprep enables rapid deployment to sites with standard hardware. SMS upgrades multiple computers running Windows NT 3.51, NT 4.0, 98, or 95 OSR2.x with the SMS client agent, enabling wide-area, centralized upgrades. RIS automatically installs Windows 2000 Professional over a network from a central server, without requiring hardware-specific images; security settings are configured post-installation via a unique SID generated for each machine. RIS requires client computers to boot over the network via a PXE-enabled NIC or supported network card, and the server must be Windows 2000 Server with access to DNS, DHCP, and Active Directory services. Microsoft released editions of Windows 2000 for different markets: Professional, Server, Advanced Server, and Datacenter Server. Windows 2000 Professional is the client version for businesses and power users, offering greater security and stability than prior desktop versions, supporting up to two processors and 4 GB of RAM, with minimum system requirements of a Pentium processor (133 MHz or higher), 32 MB RAM, 650 MB hard drive space, and a CD-ROM drive (recommended: Pentium II, 128 MB RAM, 2 GB hard drive, CD-ROM). It can be installed on 4th-generation x86 CPUs like the 80486. Windows 2000 Embedded and Windows 2000 Professional Embedded/Windows 2000 Professional for Embedded Systems are embedded versions designed for ATMs, vending machines, and similar devices; Windows 2000 Embedded was canceled in favor of Windows XP Embedded, but binary-identical FES versions were released for embedded licensing. Windows 2000 Server shares the same user interface as Professional but includes server components for infrastructure and application roles. A major new component is Active Directory, an enterprise directory service based on LDAP. Microsoft also integrated Kerberos authentication, replacing NTLM, enabling transitive trust between domains in a forest. Windows 2000 Server includes a Domain Name Server for dynamic IP address registration. It supports up to four processors and 4 GB of RAM, with a minimum requirement of 12 MHz.

Windows 2000 Embedded was cancelled during development in favor of Windows XP Embedded, although binary-identical FES versions were released and function exactly like their retail counterparts, but are licensed for embedded use. Windows 2000 Server shares the same user interface as Windows 2000 Professional and includes additional components for server roles and infrastructure and application software, with Active Directory—an enterprise-wide directory service based on LDAP—being a major new feature. Microsoft also integrated Kerberos network authentication, replacing the previously criticized NTLM system, enabling a purely transitive-trust relationship between domains in a forest, which consists of one or more domains sharing a common schema, configuration, and global catalog with two-way transitive trusts. Windows 2000 Server includes a Domain Name Server for dynamic IP address registration, supports up to 4 processors and 4 GB of RAM, with a minimum requirement of 128 MB of RAM and 1 GB of hard disk space, though requirements may increase based on installed components. Windows 2000 Server Embedded and Windows 2000 Server for Embedded Systems are binary-identical versions targeted at the embedded market, functioning identically to the retail version but licensed for embedded use. Windows 2000 Advanced Server is designed for medium-to-large businesses, supporting up to 8 CPUs, up to 8 GB of RAM on PAE systems, 8-way SMP, TCP/IP load balancing, and enhanced two-node clustering built on Microsoft Cluster Server. System requirements are similar to Windows 2000 Server, though higher for larger infrastructures. Windows 2000 Datacenter Server is designed for large businesses handling large volumes of sensitive data, supporting clustering, failover, and load balancing; it has minimum requirements similar to Advanced Server but is built for advanced, fault-tolerant, and scalable hardware, such as up to 32 CPUs and 32 GB of RAM, with rigorous testing, hardware partitioning, and change control. It was released to manufacturing on August 11, 2000, and launched on September 26, 2000, based on Windows 2000 with Service Pack 1 and was not available at retail. Windows 2000 received four full service packs and one rollup update package after SP4, the last service pack; Microsoft cancelled a planned fifth service pack and instead released Update Rollup 1 for SP4, which includes security-related hotfixes and some significant issues but excludes non-security hotfixes and undergoes less regression testing than a full service pack. Microsoft stated this update better meets customer needs, helps secure systems, reduces support costs, and supports existing hardware. Several components of Windows 2000 can be upgraded to later versions, and major Microsoft applications are available. During the Windows 2000 era, attacks increasingly came from remote Internet sources, with many malicious programs exploiting IIS services, particularly buffer overflow vulnerabilities—configuration-specific rather than OS-specific—and a common criticism is that default installations include numerous security issues, such as unnecessary enabled services and no active local security policy. According to the SANS Institute, remotely exploitable buffer overflow vulnerabilities are the most common flaws, and vulnerable encryption techniques are also criticized. Code Red and Code Red II worms exploited vulnerabilities in the Windows Indexing Service of IIS, and in August 2003, Sobig and Blaster infected over half a million Windows computers. The 2005 Zotob worm compromised Windows 2000 systems at ABC, CNN, the New York Times Company, and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. On September 8, 2009, Microsoft skipped patching two of five flaws in a monthly update, citing that fixing one critical vulnerability was "infeasible" due to the lack of TCP/IP protection architecture in Windows 2000 SP4, which would require re-architecting the OS and risking application compatibility; no patches were released for newer Windows XP versions either, and Microsoft recommended enabling Windows Firewall. Windows 2000 and its Server edition were superseded by Windows Server 2003 and Windows XP Professional, respectively. The Windows 2000 family moved from mainstream support to extended support on June 30, 2005, during which Microsoft provided only critical security updates monthly and paid per-incident support, with no new service packs or non-security updates. Extended support ended on July 13, 2010, after which no new security updates or hotfixes were provided. Updated versions of components like Windows Media Player 11 and Internet Explorer 7 were not released for Windows 2000, as Microsoft noted that security work in IE7 relies on XP SP2 functionality not feasible to port back. Users of Windows 2000 could purchase upgrade licenses for Windows Vista Business or Windows Server 2008, but neither supports direct upgrade from Windows 2000; a clean install or a two-step upgrade via XP/2003 is required, and no upgrade path exists to Windows 7. Despite being the last NT-based Windows version without product activation, Microsoft introduced Windows Genuine Advantage for certain downloads and non-critical updates. Windows 2000 reached end-of-life on July 13, 2010, alongside Windows XP SP2, and will not receive new security updates or hotfixes after that date. In Japan, over 130,000 servers and 500,000 PCs in local governments were affected, with many citing lack of funds to replace systems. As of 2011, Windows Update still supported Windows 2000 updates available on July 2010 Patch Tuesday, if older optional features are enabled later; Internet Explorer 6 under Windows 2000 did not receive security patches after its end of support, unlike IE6 on Windows XP. The Windows Malicious Software Removal Tool, available monthly for XP and later, can still be manually downloaded for Windows 2000. In 2020, Microsoft disabled Windows Update for SHA-1 endpoints for older versions, and since Windows 2000 lacked a SHA-2 update, Windows Update services were discontinued as of late July 2020. As of March 2024, many old Windows 2000 updates remain available on the Microsoft Update Catalog, and a third-party tool named Legacy Update allows installation from the catalog. An independent project named Windows Update Restored, available since 2022, aims to restore Windows Update websites for older versions, including Windows 2000. In October 2002, Microsoft commissioned IDC to compare the total cost of ownership (TCO) of enterprise applications on Windows 2000 versus Linux over five years for an average organization of 100 employees. IDC found Windows 2000 had a better TCO in file, print, network infrastructure, and security infrastructure, but Linux had a better TCO for web serving. The greatest cost was staffing and downtime, with Linux servers showing less unplanned downtime than Windows 2000 servers, running less workload per server, and no businesses using 4-way SMP Linux systems. The report emphasized that TCO is only one factor in choosing an IT platform and noted that improved management and server software could alter the findings.
